packages/show-planner/src/cache.ts.content: `PlanCache` has no eviction policy (no max size, TTL, or LRU). Because a fresh entry is created for every distinct combination of track fingerprint / planner version / style / venue / config, a long-lived instance accumulates entries indefinitely and grows memory without bound. Consider bounding the store (e.g. cap + LRU eviction or TTL) so a long-running process cannot leak.

The composite key collapses five inputs into a single 32-bit hash (`fnv1aHex` returns only 8 hex chars / 32 bits). The string inputs themselves are properly delimited by `stableStringify` (arrays/quotes), so the only collision source is the truncated hash space: ~2^16 distinct keys already hit a ~50% birthday collision rate. A collision silently returns another plan's value (stale/incorrect plan) with no verification. For a correctness-critical cache, key on the full `stableStringify` output or use a wider digest (e.g. 64/128-bit) rather than a 32-bit FNV.

packages/track-model/src/index.ts.content: Identity priority is inconsistent between the guard and the generated id. This line (and the file header comment documenting §12 as native ID → path → file hash → PCM fingerprint) resolves the path *before* the hash, but the `id` ternary below resolves `fileHash`/`pcmFingerprint` *before* the path. A track that carries both a `seratoPath`/`canonicalPath` and a `fileHash` therefore gets a `hash:…` id even though it was validated/memoized under the path key (see `identity-service.ts`, which uses this same `key` order for its cache). The same logical track can also yield two different ids depending on which parts a caller supplies (path-only vs path+hash), breaking stable identity resolution.

packages/track-model/src/index.ts.content: `coverageOf` is a second readiness implementation that diverges from the authoritative one. `computeReadiness` (`packages/analysis-client/src/readiness.ts`, mirrored from `readiness.py`) derives the level purely from the input map; here `full` additionally requires `sections.length > 0`, and the structured branch below ignores the model's declared `analysisCoverage`/`readinessLevel`/`analysisCoverage2.level` entirely. Consequently `coverageOf` can return a level that disagrees with the model's own declared coverage — e.g. a model with `analysisCoverage === "full"` and no sections reports `"structured"`, and a model declaring `"structured"` with an empty grid reports `"adaptive"`. The UI readiness badge (`resolve-live.ts`, `library-rows.ts`, `live-fields.ts`) can then contradict the level the analysis worker issued. Derive from the declared level / `analysisCoverage2.inputs`, or document this as an intentionally coarse heuristic.

`Coverage` duplicates the `ReadinessLevel` union already exported by `@autolight/contracts` (`readinessLevelSchema`), a package this module already imports types from. Two identical unions risk drifting apart; import and reuse `ReadinessLevel` instead of redefining the type here.

The sum `w[0]+w[1]` is 1 by construction (splitWeights always sets `weights[1] = 1 - weights[0]`), so the first assertion is tautological, and `w[0] > 0.3` is an arbitrary threshold that a completely flat/no-ramp feather (`f` constant) also satisfies. No cell on the split line is checked against 0.5, so a broken/mis-shaped feather passes. `resolveSelector` returns `string[]` on every code path (all branches build and return arrays), so `Array.isArray(zone)` is always true and validates nothing. protocol-fixtures/rekordbox/ax/windows-t.content: Deck 2's child schema diverges from Deck 1: it is missing the `remaining` Text element and its Button sits at `position: 3` instead of Deck 1's `position: 4`. Any consumer that indexes deck children by absolute position (e.g. `children[3]` for the transport button) or expects a fixed field set (title/artist/elapsed/remaining/button) will misread Deck 2 — reading the Play button as the remaining-time Text — or throw/index-miss. Since this fixture is meant to be representative protocol input, either keep both decks structurally identical (add the `remaining` Text and shift the Button to position 4) or make the parser explicitly tolerant of missing elements.

Elapsed-time format is inconsistent: Deck 1 uses a signed value (`+0:12`) while Deck 2 uses an unsigned value (`1:05`). A parser that assumes the leading sign (or a duration parser that concatenates elapsed/remaining using the sign convention) will misparse Deck 2, and conversely this fixture would let a parser that only handles the unsigned form pass while failing on real Rekordbox output. Normalize the format across decks (e.g. `+1:05`) or ensure the parser is explicitly tested against both forms.

Both AX tree fixtures (`windows-tree.json` and `macos-tree.json`) are explicitly hand-authored/synthetic ('Not a hardware capture'), yet they are registered as the only fixtures for the `ax/v1` decoder and consumed by tests as if they were recorded trees. Tests driven by them can pass against an invented structure and mask genuine parser defects (missing elements, different ordering, inverted labels). Runbook HW-RB-AX-01 has not run (per STATUS.md). Record the unverified status in the fixtures (e.g., a `capture: synthetic` or `verified: false` key) and generate/validate against the real UIA/AX dumps before relying on them as protocol evidence.

apps/desktop/electron/services/base.ts.content: Stale/contradictory lifecycle timestamps across a stop/start cycle. Because `startedAtMs` is assigned with `??=`, once set it is never refreshed: a service that is stopped and started again (e.g. LifecycleService.start() -> stop() -> start()) will report the very first start time in `status()`. Additionally `stoppedAtMs` is only cleared for running/degraded, so a transition into `starting`/`idle` after a stop leaves both a stale `stoppedAtMs` and a stale `startedAtMs` in the snapshot, and any invalid transition (e.g. `idle -> stopped`, or `failed -> running` without a fresh start) is silently accepted. Refresh the start timestamp when entering a running/degraded state from a non-running one.

Two issues here. (1) An explicit but empty string is returned as-is (only `undefined` is rejected), so a caller passing `""` gets a bogus empty path; downstream callers such as SecretsService.blobFile() then do `join("", "secrets.enc.json")`, producing a path relative to the CWD instead of the userData dir. (2) The bare `catch` swallows every failure from both the `electron` import AND `app.getPath("userData")`, so a genuine getPath error is indistinguishable from 'electron not installed' and silently degrades to 'no userData dir'. Reject empty strings and narrow the catch to the import step.

`messageOf` only special-cases `Error`; for plain structured error payloads (e.g. `{ code, message }` objects passed from typed error paths) `String(err)` yields `"[object Object]"`, so the honest reason that should land in `ServiceStatus.detail` / `ServiceError.error.message` is lost. Handle objects exposing a string `message`.

apps/desktop/journeys/m1-slice.journey.t.content: Two issues with the blackout deadline: (1) `t0.wallMs` is `Date.now()` captured in the Playwright test-runner process, while `zero.sentAtMs` is the recording transport's timestamp from the main process — if the transport uses a monotonic/app-relative clock (the `RecordedFrame` type gives no guarantee), the `< 100 ms` subtraction mixes clock domains and is meaningless. (2) `frames` is read once immediately after the keypress with no retry, so the blackout frame may not be recorded yet, making `expect(zero).not.toBeNull()` flaky. Confirm both timestamps share one epoch and poll/wait for the zero frame before asserting the deadline.

This assertion is tautological: `resume.wallMs` and `t0.wallMs` are both `Date.now()` and the A press necessarily happens after the B press, so it can never fail and validates nothing about "resume on the next bar". Either drop it or assert something meaningful (e.g. that a non-black frame resumes after `resume.wallMs` in the next recorded frames).

The P-56 continuity check is too weak: it only requires at least one frame with `sentAtMs > lastBefore` and pairwise gaps `< 500 ms` starting from index 1. A single frame emitted right after the freeze begins satisfies it, and the gap between `lastBefore` and the first "during" frame is never checked, so a stall at the start of the pause goes undetected. Also, nothing computes that frames actually span the full 5 s freeze window (or the expected frame count for the qualified rate), and the negative-gap case (unsorted `sentAtMs`) would also pass. Assert frame coverage across the whole pause window (first/last timestamps vs. the freeze duration and expected count).

apps/desktop/journeys/night.journey.ts.content: This assertion cannot tell a working blackout from a broken one. `renderFrame` (packages/renderer/src/index.ts:108-137) already returns an all-zero frame for any cell not covered by an active lighting cue, and the only cue here is the blackout itself. If the `blackout` type were dropped/ignored (or `intensity: 1` were mishandled) the fixtures would still render `rgb(0,0,0)` and this test would pass green. Add a lower-priority lit look on the same cells (e.g. a `section-look` on `PRIMARY` with `priority: < 100`) so the frame is black *only because* blackout overrides it, and assert those cells are non-black without the blackout cue.

The test claims to prove crossfade "hands over ownership", but it never asserts `owner`, and it cannot observe which deck dominates: the single fixture (`makeFixture("f", 4)` + `groups: ["PRIMARY", "SECONDARY"]`) belongs to both target groups, so deck A and deck B paint the *same* cells and `brightness` counts the same lit cells on both sides. The only real check is the weight ordering, which would still pass even if ownership failed to transfer. Assert the handover explicitly, e.g. `expect(left.owner).toBe("a")` / `expect(right.owner).toBe("b")`, and give A and B distinct fixtures so the dominant deck's cells can be distinguished.

In production `deckA` and `mixA.state` are the *same* object (`resolve-live.ts:80` builds `mixA: { state: deckA, ... }`), but here `makeDeck` is called twice, so `deckA !== mixA.state` (and `deckB !== mixB.state`). The view-model reads `deckA` for `weights` and `mixA.state` inside `mixDown`, so these duplicated-but-identical instances no longer mirror the production shape and could mask a state-synchronization regression. Build one instance per deck and reuse it for both `deckX` and `mixX.state`.
